page: Alibaba Cloud ecs.u2i-c1m4.3xlarge is a general-purpose virtual server built on the KVM hypervisor and powered by x86_64 Intel Xeon processors running at a nominal clock speed of 2.7 GHz. The instance is provisioned with 12 dedicated vCPUs and 48.0 GB of memory, maintaining a standard 1:4 vCPU-to-memory ratio of 4.0 GB per vCPU. It does not include hardware accelerators such as GPUs.

Network connectivity features a baseline network bandwidth of 8 Gbps, though it does not come with complimentary public IPv4 addresses. In terms of storage architecture, the instance provides no local storage disks, requiring external cloud block storage for persistent operating system and application data volumes. This design provides data persistence across host migrations at the expense of needing network-attached disk provisioning.

From a cost-efficiency perspective, the balanced core-to-memory allocation makes it effective for horizontal application scaling where resource demands match standard enterprise distributions. Workload suitability includes multi-tier web application servers, containerized microservices, build nodes in CI/CD pipelines, enterprise resource planning modules, and mid-tier backend databases.
description: Alibaba Cloud ecs.u2i-c1m4.3xlarge is a general-purpose virtual machine based on the x86_64 architecture and KVM hypervisor. Powered by Intel Xeon processors operating at 2.7 GHz, the server delivers 12 dedicated vCPUs paired with 48.0 GB of system memory, matching an industry-standard 1:4 core-to-memory ratio of 4.0 GB per core. The instance operates without integrated local disk storage or hardware GPU accelerators, relying on remote block storage solutions for disk operations and root filesystems. With a baseline network capacity of 8 Gbps and no bundled public IPv4 addresses, it delivers stable inter-service and cloud network throughput. The balanced balance of compute capacity and RAM qualifies it for enterprise business applications, container hosts, intermediate data caching, CI/CD execution environments, and transactional relational database workloads.
